--- Page 1 ---
SpecPrefetch: Parameter-Efficient Expert Prefetching for Sparse MoE
Foundation Models
Jinwei Kong1,2,*
Runqi Meng2,*
Fanyi Wang1
Wentao Qiu1,3
Haotian Hu1
Yongjian Zhou4
Zhenhua Ge1,†
1 StepOs
2 ShanghaiTech University
3 Xiamen University
4 Chongqing University
kongjw2023@shanghaitech.edu.cn
gezhenhua@ustc.edu
* Equal contribution.
† Corresponding author.
Abstract
Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models ex-
pand foundation model capacity through condi-
tional expert activation, but their full expert
pools remain difficult to deploy under lim-
ited accelerator memory. Although expert of-
floading alleviates memory pressure by mov-
ing inactive experts to host memory or stor-
age, it introduces a routing-dependent trans-
fer bottleneck: required experts are known
only after native top-K routing, which serial-
izes routing, expert loading, and expert execu-
tion during inference. To address this bottle-
neck, we propose SpecPrefetch, a parameter-
efficient prefetching framework for offloaded
MoE inference. SpecPrefetch uses a shared
lightweight adapter to predict next-layer ex-
pert candidates only for asynchronous trans-
fer, while the frozen native router still deter-
mines the final executed experts. By separat-
ing transfer prediction from execution routing,
SpecPrefetch reduces exposed expert-loading
latency without changing pretrained routing
semantics, so prediction errors affect transfer
efficiency rather than model outputs. In ad-
dition, a window-aware scheduler prioritizes
feasible transfers under cache and bandwidth
constraints. Across Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B and
DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny, SpecPrefetch achieves
the best average expert recall in 9 out of 10
model-benchmark settings with substantially
fewer trainable parameters than learned pre-
dictor baselines.
On a Snapdragon 8 Elite
device, SpecPrefetch further improves decod-
ing throughput by up to 20% over a compute-
optimized offloading runtime, demonstrating
practical benefits for storage-constrained MoE
deployment. The code and model weights are
available at https://github.com/wei390/
SpecPrefetch.
1
Introduction
Recent progress in large language models (LLMs)
and vision language models (VLMs) has been
driven by scaling model capacity, training data,
and computation. However, dense scaling increas-
ingly strains inference cost, memory capacity, and
serving throughput. Mixture of Experts (MoE)
architectures provide an attractive alternative by
expanding total parameter capacity while activat-
ing only a small subset of experts for each token.
Modern MoE models organize expert computation
through pure routed expert pools or shared plus
routed expert designs (Qwen Team, 2025; Jiang
et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2024). Despite architec-
tural differences, both designs expose the same de-
ployment bottleneck. Sparse activation reduces per
token computation, but the full expert pool must
still be stored or made accessible during inference.
As foundation models move from cloud datacen-
ters to commodity GPUs and edge platforms, this
storage-computation gap becomes a critical bottle-
neck under limited memory, and local compute.
Expert offloading provides a natural response
to the dense expert footprint of MoE models un-
der memory constrained deployment. Instead of
keeping the entire expert pool resident on the accel-
erator, offloading places inactive experts in CPU
memory or host-side storage and transfers selected
experts to the active device on demand. However,
expert demand is not known statically. In each
MoE layer, the top-k experts are determined only
after the preceding hidden states are computed and
evaluated by the router. As a result, expert transfer
cannot be issued until the routing decision becomes
available, which serializes hidden state computa-
tion, routing, host-to-device transfer, and expert
execution along the inference critical path. Thus,
the central challenge is not only reducing transfer
cost, but also revealing expert demand early enough
to overlap transfer with ongoing computation.
As shown in Figure 1, existing approaches mit-
igate exposed expert-transfer latency from three
perspectives, but their design choices introduce dif-
ferent limitations. Transfer-cost reduction methods,
such as quantization and compression, reduce the
1
arXiv:2607.24787v1  [cs.AI]  24 Jun 2026


--- Page 2 ---
Figure 1: Comparison of expert-transfer strategies in
offloaded MoE inference.
communication volume of expert movement (Yan
et al., 2025). However, they do not alter the timing
at which expert demand becomes available: re-
quired experts are still identified only after native
top-K routing, so expert transfer remains serialized
after routing and can still lie on the critical path
before expert execution. Training-free prefetching
methods, represented by FATE, exploit cross-layer
routing regularity to anticipate expert demand with-
out parameter updates (Fang et al., 2025b). While
lightweight and portable, their prediction accuracy
depends on stable routing correlations, which may
not consistently hold across model architectures,
tasks, and modalities. Training-based prediction
methods estimate expert activations using auxil-
iary predictors, parameter-efficient tuning, draft
modules, or pre-gating mechanisms (Hwang et al.,
2024; Chen et al., 2025; Leviathan et al., 2023; Li
et al., 2024). Although these methods can improve
expert recall, coupling prediction with routing or
execution may perturb the original expert activa-
tion pattern and potentially affect model behavior.
Therefore, an effective prefetching solution should
predict next-layer expert demand early for transfer
scheduling, remain parameter-efficient, and pre-
serve native routing for final expert selection.
To address these limitations,
we propose
SpecPrefetch,
a
parameter-efficient
prefetch-
ing framework for offloaded MoE inference.
SpecPrefetch formulates prefetching as next-layer
expert prediction: given the representation at layer
l, a shared lightweight adapter predicts a com-
pact candidate set for layer l + 1.
The candi-
dates are used only for asynchronous host-to-device
transfer, while the native router at layer l + 1
still selects the final top-K experts for execution.
By decoupling transfer prediction from execution
routing, SpecPrefetch improves expert availabil-
ity without altering pretrained routing semantics.
At runtime, a window-aware scheduler turns pre-
dicted candidates into feasible transfer decisions
by considering prediction confidence, cache resi-
dency, and transfer completion time. We validate
SpecPrefetch through both offline expert predic-
tion experiments and real-device mobile evaluation.
Across Qwen- and DeepSeek-style MoE architec-
tures, SpecPrefetch improves next-layer expert cov-
erage with low trainable overhead; on a mobile de-
vice, it further translates prediction gains into prac-
tical latency reduction under storage-constrained
offloaded inference.
To summarize, we make the following contribu-
tions:
• We identify learned transfer-only prefetching
as a distinct design point for offloaded MoE
inference.
• We develop SpecPrefetch, a lightweight
adapter-based framework that predicts next-
layer experts and schedules feasible asyn-
chronous transfers under runtime constraints.
• We validate SpecPrefetch through offline pre-
diction experiments and real-device mobile
evaluation, showing higher expert coverage,
low trainable overhead, and practical latency
reduction.
2
Related Work
2.1
Sparse MoE Foundation Models
Mixture of Experts (MoE) scales foundation mod-
els through conditional computation. In sparse
MoE layers, a router activates only a small sub-
set of experts for each token, increasing total pa-
rameter capacity while limiting activated compu-
tation (Shazeer et al., 2017). Early systems such
as GShard, Switch Transformer, and GLaM show
that sparse routing improves model capacity and
language modeling performance with controlled
computation cost, while introducing challenges in
routing stability, load balancing, communication,
and expert specialization (Lepikhin et al., 2021;
Fedus et al., 2022; Du et al., 2022).
Recent MoE models further diversify expert
architecture. Mixtral uses a pure routed expert
pool (Jiang et al., 2024), DeepSeekMoE sepa-
rates shared and routed experts (Dai et al., 2024),
and sparse upcycling initializes MoE models from
dense checkpoints to reduce training cost (Ko-
matsuzaki et al., 2023). These designs differ in
2


--- Page 3 ---
how expert capacity is constructed, shared, and
routed, which directly affects offloading and expert
prefetching.
2.2
Offloaded MoE Inference and Expert
Prefetching
Expert offloading enables large sparse MoE models
to run under limited accelerator memory by keep-
ing inactive experts in CPU memory or host-side
storage. Existing systems reduce GPU memory
pressure through expert caching, placement, asyn-
chronous transfer, and heterogeneous memory man-
agement (Shen et al., 2022; Xue et al., 2024; He
et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025a; Fang et al., 2025a).
One line of work reduces expert movement cost or
frequency: cache-based methods retain frequently
or recently used experts on the accelerator (Xue
et al., 2024; Kamahori et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024),
while quantization, compression, expert splitting,
and fine-grained placement reduce transfer volume
or improve cache flexibility (Yan et al., 2025; Tang
et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025b). These methods
improve memory efficiency, but mainly optimize
expert movement after demand is known.
Another line of work overlaps expert movement
with computation through scheduling and prefetch-
ing.
ExpertFlow, Klotski, LayerScope, and re-
lated systems use predictive scheduling, token re-
batching, asynchronous I/O, pipeline execution,
and expert-aware memory organization to improve
MoE serving (He et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2025a; Yu
et al., 2025a; Abhimanyu Bambhaniya, 2024; Sun
and Li, 2025). FATE further uses adjacent-layer
gate information for training-free expert prefetch-
ing in edge inference (Fang et al., 2025b). These
methods show the value of prefetching, but training-
free prediction depends on stable cross-layer rout-
ing regularity, and many scheduling systems focus
on throughput-oriented serving with batching or
token-flow reorganization.
Training-based methods estimate expert acti-
vations with learned routers, auxiliary predic-
tors, pre-gating mechanisms, or parameter-efficient
adaptation (Hwang et al., 2024; Chen et al.,
2025; Gavhane et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025).
Speculative generation methods create additional
scheduling windows through draft-then-verify ex-
ecution (Leviathan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024;
Wang et al., 2025). In contrast, SpecPrefetch tar-
gets standard offloaded MoE execution: it predicts
next-layer candidate experts only for transfer prepa-
ration, while the native router still selects the final
top-K experts. Thus, SpecPrefetch changes when
experts are moved, not which experts are executed.
3
Method
SpecPrefetch is a parameter-efficient prefetching
framework for offloaded MoE inference that antic-
ipates the expert demand of layer l + 1 from the
router input available at layer l. As illustrated in
Figure 2, the predicted candidates are used only for
asynchronous transfer preparation, while the native
router still selects the final top-K experts during
execution, so SpecPrefetch hides exposed trans-
fer latency without changing the routing semantics
of the pretrained MoE model. Following this de-
sign, Section 3.1 first formulates router-preserving
next-layer expert prefetching as a transfer-only
prediction problem; Section 3.2 then introduces
a lightweight next-layer gate calibration module to
estimate expert priorities of layer l + 1 from the
representation available at layer l; and Section 3.3
finally describes a window-aware runtime sched-
uler that converts predicted priorities into feasible
asynchronous transfers under cache, queue, and
bandwidth constraints.

routed experts per layer. Let Xj

3.2
Adapter-Based Expert Prediction
We implement the predictor P l with a single
lightweight external adapter shared by the predic-
tion branch. The pretrained MoE forward path
is kept frozen, including all native routers and
routed experts. Given the router input at layer l,
the adapter estimates the expert priorities of layer
l+1 only for prefetch ranking. It does not calibrate,
replace, or participate in the native router during
execution.

(b, s) at layer l. The shared adapter predicts next-
layer expert logits through a low-rank mapping:

3.3
Window-Aware Runtime Scheduling
Finally, the window-aware scheduler turns pre-
dicted next-layer expert priorities into asyn-
chronous host-to-device transfers. For each anchor
layer l, it receives the priority scores {sl+1
e
}E
e=1
and candidate set Cl+1. The scheduler maintains
the resident expert set G(t), the pending transfer
set U(t), and the transfer queue Q(t), with each
expert indexed by the layer-expert pair (l + 1, e).
At scheduling time t, the scheduler estimates
whether each candidate can arrive before the tar-
get layer begins routed expert computation. Let

moved to G(t) after transfer completion.
When execution reaches layer l + 1, experts al-
ready in G(t) are executed immediately; otherwise,
they are loaded on demand. We measure prefetch
effectiveness by ready recall:

Ready recall measures the fraction of native-router-
selected experts that are resident before routed ex-
pert computation begins. Since the scheduler only
controls expert placement, unused prefetches or
on-demand loads affect efficiency but not the pre-
trained MoE output.
4
Experiment
4.1
Experimental Setup
Models
and
Benchmarks.
We
evaluate
SpecPrefetch
on
two
representative
MoE
foundation models, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B and
DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny, which cover different sparse
expert architectures and routing behaviors. The
benchmarks are organized into two workload
groups.
The VLM group includes ChartQA
Test, OCRBench, and HallusionBench, covering
text-rich visual understanding and multimodal
hallucination evaluation. The LLM group includes
GSM8K and HumanEval, covering mathematical
reasoning and code generation. This setting allows
us to evaluate next-layer expert prediction across
model families and workload modalities.
Baselines.
We compare SpecPrefetch with three
representative expert prediction baselines: FATE,
Draft Model, and ProMoE. FATE represents
training-free cross-layer prediction based on rout-
ing regularity, Draft Model uses an auxiliary pre-
dictor to estimate next-layer expert demand, and
ProMoE represents a stronger learned predictor
with a larger prediction module. For fair compar-
ison, all predictors are evaluated under the same
transfer-only prefetching protocol: predicted ex-
perts are used only for prefetching, while the native
router determines the executed experts.
System
Evaluation
Settings.
We
evaluate
system-level performance through both simulation
experiments and real-device mobile evaluation.
The simulation experiments are conducted on
Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B and DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny to
quantify how next-layer expert prediction reduces
exposed transfer latency and improves end-to-end
inference speedup under controlled offloading
settings.
In these simulations, inactive experts
reside in host-side memory or storage, and selected
experts are transferred to accelerator memory
according to native router demand. We further
deploy DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny on a Qualcomm
Snapdragon 8 Elite device with an Adreno 825
GPU for real-device mobile evaluation, where the
decoding pipeline runs on device and different
storage-speed regimes are emulated by injecting
controlled I/O latency into expert loading.
Evaluation Metrics.
We evaluate each method
from three perspectives: expert prediction quality,
parameter overhead, and system efficiency. For ex-
pert prediction quality, we report next-layer expert
coverage recall. Given the native batch level expert
demand T l+1 at the next MoE layer and the pre-
dicted candidate expert set Cl+1, expert coverage

Implementation.
We use AdamW with β =
(0.9, 0.999), ϵ = 10−8, learning rate 10−4, cosine
scheduling, warmup ratio 0.03, gradient clipping
of 0.5, bf16 precision, and train for one epoch. The
maximum text length is set to 4096 for DeepSeek-
VL2-Tiny and 2048 for Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B. All
experiments are implemented with PyTorch, Hug-
gingFace Trainer, DeepSpeed, and FlashAttention
2, and are conducted on 2 × 8 NVIDIA A800-
SXM4-80GB GPUs.

Overall, SpecPrefetch shows the most stable ad-
vantage on VLM workloads and remains stronger
than training-based baselines in most settings. For
instance, on DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny HumanEval, it
improves the average recall from 78.54% for Draft
Model and 75.07% for ProMoE to 89.13%. These
results demonstrate more reliable next-layer expert
coverage across model families, candidate budgets,
and workload modalities.
4.3
Ablation and Parameter Efficiency
Ablation on predictor design.
We isolate the
effect of adapter-based calibration by comparing
SpecPrefetch with an MLP Predictor trained un-
der the same next-layer expert supervision. While
the MLP Predictor learns a generic mapping from
current-layer representations to next-layer expert
demand, SpecPrefetch calibrates the frozen target-
layer gate with a lightweight adapter, making the
comparison focus on the benefit of gate-aware pre-
diction.
Tables 2 and 3 show consistent gains over
the MLP Predictor.
On Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B,
SpecPrefetch improves average recall by +4.94%
on GSM8K and +11.62% on HumanEval, and also
improves all VLM workloads. On DeepSeek-VL2-
Figure 3: Real-device decoding throughput under differ-
ent storage-speed settings. Higher values indicate better
end-to-end token generation performance.
Tiny, the gains are larger, reaching +18.71% on
GSM8K and +28.33% on HumanEval, with more
than +8% improvement across all VLM workloads.
These results show that gate-aware adapter cali-
bration provides more reliable next-layer expert
coverage than a generic learned predictor.
Parameter overhead comparison.
To examine
whether the recall gains come from larger predic-
tors, Table 4 compares the trainable parameter over-
head of different predictor designs. On DeepSeek-
VL2-Tiny, SpecPrefetch uses 1.63M trainable pa-
rameters, which is only 0.07M more than Single
MLP, but far smaller than Draft Model and ProMoE
with 26.40M and 32.69M parameters. This corre-
sponds to only 6.2% and 5.0% of their trainable
parameter counts, respectively.
The advantage is more evident on Qwen3-VL-
MoE-30B. SpecPrefetch uses 12.95M trainable pa-
rameters, compared with 24.38M for Single MLP,
19.19M for Draft Model, and 414.45M for Pro-
MoE. In particular, SpecPrefetch requires only
3.1% of the trainable parameters of ProMoE. These
results indicate that SpecPrefetch improves next-
layer expert prediction through parameter efficient
adapter based calibration rather than predictor scal-
ing, which is essential for prefetching because pre-
dictor overhead should not offset the latency saved
by asynchronous transfer.
4.4
Real-Device Mobile Evaluation
We further evaluate whether next-layer expert pre-
diction can translate into practical latency reduction
on resource-constrained devices. The experiments
are conducted with DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny on a Qual-
comm Snapdragon 8 Elite device with an Adreno
825 GPU. The model uses 4-bit groupwise quan-
7


--- Page 8 ---
Figure 4: Speedup of the compute-optimized runtime
and SpecPrefetch relative to load-on-demand execution
across storage-speed settings.
Figure 5: Cold-cache real-device throughput after clear-
ing the operating-system page cache before each run.
tized experts and contains 11 MoE layers, each
with 64 routed experts and K = 6 routed experts
per token. Each quantized expert occupies 1.94
MB, resulting in 1.36 GB total expert storage. We
compare three configurations: a load-on-demand
baseline, a compute-optimized runtime that batches
expert dispatch, and SpecPrefetch built on top of
the compute-optimized runtime. For each configu-
ration, we decode 30 tokens and report the average
over five runs. Since DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny follows
a shared-plus-routed expert design, its shared ex-
pert remains resident and provides a compute win-
dow that can partially overlap with routed expert
loading.
Figure 3 and Figure 4 report throughput and
speedup under different storage speeds. Under
the fastest NVMe setting, SpecPrefetch brings lim-
ited additional gain, with the compute-optimized
runtime and SpecPrefetch reaching 4.36 and 4.31
tokens per second, respectively. This is expected
because hot-cache routed-expert reads take only
about 0.15 ms, much shorter than the 2.0 ms res-
ident shared-expert computation, so most I/O la-
tency is already hidden by computation overlap.
As storage becomes slower, routed-expert loading
exceeds this overlap window and appears on the
critical path. In this regime, SpecPrefetch improves
throughput over the compute-optimized runtime by
+15%, +20%, and +17% under Mid UFS, Slow
UFS, and SD Card settings, respectively, showing
that prefetching addresses exposed expert-loading
latency that batching and fused dispatch alone can-
not remove.
Figure 5 evaluates a stricter first-run scenario by
clearing the operating-system page cache before
each run. Under cold cache, routed expert loading
can no longer be fully hidden by the shared ex-
pert computation window. As a result, the baseline
and compute-optimized runtime achieve similar
throughput, 3.29 and 3.25 tokens per second, show-
ing that compute-side optimization alone does not
remove the storage bottleneck. SpecPrefetch with
compute optimization reaches 3.76 tokens per sec-
ond, corresponding to a 1.14× speedup over the
baseline and a +16% prefetch contribution. These
results show that SpecPrefetch is most effective
when routed expert loading is exposed on the crit-
ical path. Its benefit comes from preparing next-
layer routed experts before they are needed, rather
than accelerating expert computation itself.
5
Conclusion
We presented SpecPrefetch, a parameter-efficient
prefetching framework for offloaded MoE infer-
ence. SpecPrefetch uses a shared adapter to predict
next-layer expert demand only for asynchronous
transfer, while the native router still determines
final expert selection. This transfer-only design re-
duces exposed host-to-device or storage latency
without changing pretrained routing semantics.
Across pure routed and shared-plus-routed MoE
models, SpecPrefetch improves expert recall over
MLP, draft-model, and ProMoE-style predictors
with substantially fewer trainable parameters. Real-
device evaluation on Snapdragon 8 Elite further
shows that these prediction gains translate into
higher decoding throughput when routed expert
loading lies on the critical path. These results high-
light lightweight next-layer expert prediction as a
practical mechanism for memory- and bandwidth-
constrained MoE deployment.

--- Page 9 ---

Acknowledgment
We use an AI assistant for paraphrasing support
during the writing of the manuscript.
7
Limitation
SpecPrefetch has several limitations.
First, ex-
pert coverage recall is only a proxy for runtime
benefit. A correctly predicted expert improves la-
tency only when its transfer would otherwise be
exposed on the critical path; therefore, the speedup
depends on cache state, storage bandwidth, transfer-
compute overlap, and runtime support for asyn-
chronous loading. Under hot-cache or fast-storage
settings, routed expert reads may already be hid-
den by computation, leaving limited latency for
prefetching to remove. Second, although predic-
tion errors do not affect model outputs because
the native router still determines final expert selec-
tion, they can still reduce system efficiency: false
positives may waste bandwidth and cache capac-
ity, while false negatives still trigger on-demand
loading. Third, SpecPrefetch uses a single shared
adapter for parameter efficiency, which may not
fully capture layer-specific routing patterns in MoE
models with highly heterogeneous expert special-
ization. Finally, the current scheduler follows a
local feasibility-aware strategy and does not jointly
optimize global cache residency, eviction, cross-
request reuse, or multi-user batching. Our real-
device evaluation is also limited to DeepSeek-VL2-
Tiny on a mobile platform, so broader validation on
larger MoE models, different hardware backends,
and server-side offloading environments remains
necessary.

A
Appendix
A.1
Dataset Details
This section provides details of the datasets used in
our experiments. We organize the datasets into two
groups according to their roles: predictor training
datasets and evaluation benchmarks. The predictor
training datasets contain diverse visual-language
data sources covering document understanding,
OCR-centric reasoning, chart and figure interpre-
tation, image captioning, visual instruction follow-
ing, and compositional visual question answering.
The evaluation benchmarks are held-out workloads
used in the main experiments to assess next-layer
expert prediction and inference efficiency.
A.1.1
Predictor Training Datasets
The predictor training data are grouped by task
type to reflect the diversity of input structures and
prompt formats.
Document and OCR-centric visual understand-
ing.
This group includes DocVQA, Infograph-
icVQA, OCR-VQA, ST-VQA, TextVQA, and
TextCaps. These datasets focus on visual inputs
with substantial textual content, including scanned
documents, infographics, book covers, natural
scene text, and text-rich images. DocVQA and
InfographicVQA emphasize document and info-
graphic understanding, where models must reason
over visually structured text layouts. OCR-VQA,
ST-VQA, and TextVQA focus on reading and rea-
soning over text embedded in images. TextCaps
extends OCR-centric understanding to caption gen-
eration, requiring descriptions that incorporate visi-
ble text in the image.

A.1.2
Evaluation Benchmarks
The main evaluation uses held-out LLM and VLM
workloads. For VLM evaluation, we use OCR-
Bench, ChartQA-Test, and HallusionBench. OCR-
Bench focuses on OCR-related multimodal under-
standing and text-rich visual reasoning. ChartQA-
Test evaluates question answering over charts and
structured visual information.
HallusionBench
evaluates multimodal reasoning in hallucination-
sensitive scenarios. For LLM evaluation, we use
GSM8K and HumanEval. GSM8K evaluates math-
ematical reasoning, while HumanEval evaluates
code generation.
A.1.3
Dataset Summary
Overall, the dataset collection covers a broad
range of input formats, including documents, in-
fographics, scene-text images, charts, natural im-
ages, instruction-following samples, mathematical
problems, and code-generation tasks. This diver-
sity supports evaluation across heterogeneous LLM
and VLM workloads without relying on a single
task distribution.
